stories.topic: The Code That Sabotaged Iran's Centrifuges
stories.summary: Israel, long keen to disrupt Iran's nuclear programme, got into the operating system of the industrial controllers running Iran's uranium centrifuges. The code knew the frequencies the centrifuges needed. Whenever scientists told a centrifuge to do the right thing, the code made it do the wrong thing, so machines fell apart and the uranium purification failed. For a long time the Iranians thought they simply had unsolved engineering problems. Even after the sabotage was discovered, they still faced hard questions: who did it, which powers were involved, and how could they respond?
stories.insight: This is the cleanest example of an attack that stays below the detection threshold. The victim pays the full cost while believing it is bad luck, and by the time it learns the truth, attribution and retaliation are still hard.
stories.quote: So for a long time the scientists thought that we have not yet solved our R and D problems. While actually there was clever code that was disrupting them.

stories.topic: The Anchor Dragged Across the Baltic Seabed
stories.summary: Russia runs a 'shadow fleet' of tankers that carry its crude oil to friendly buyers, including China and India. A Chinese tanker in this fleet dragged its anchor along the floor of the Baltic Sea and tore through gas pipelines, oil pipelines and fibre-optic lines. A crew can simply call this an accident. This time, though, the Finnish Navy boarded the ship and detained the crew for interrogation. Ajay compares this to India capturing Kasab alive in 2008. He sees the incident as a major escalation, with Russia now using Chinese ships to harm the Baltic nations.
stories.insight: An ordinary object becomes a weapon when its use can be denied. Deniability only breaks when someone physically seizes the perpetrator and starts asking questions.
stories.quote: Even if you manage to catch it in time, you manage to catch that tanker. The tanker throws up its hands and says, oops, this was a mistake.

stories.topic: The Day Paris Lost Its Fibre
stories.summary: Russia is believed to have run a test in which about fourteen fibre-optic cables carrying internet connectivity into Paris were all cut at the same moment. It was a highly professional job by people who understood the city's entire network. In peacetime it was 'only' a nuisance that disrupted business for days. The unstated message was that the same could perhaps be done to twenty European cities.
stories.insight: Every small hybrid attack carries a veiled threat: 'if I could do this, what else could I do?' That fear changes the victim's behaviour, and it is how a weak power gets the peacemakers on the other side to argue for appeasement.
stories.quote: Somebody deeply understood all the fiber optic connectivity to Paris and cut it all at once.

stories.summary: Putin sent men in plain clothes to take over Crimea. They were nicknamed the Little Green Men because they claimed to be a local militia, not Russian soldiers, and the operation was kept tightly secret. The Obama team was fooled for a while and treated it as an internal rebellion that the US should stay out of. By the time it was clear that this was a Putin operation, the Russian army controlled Crimea.
stories.insight: Deniability does not need to fool anyone forever. It only needs to delay attribution until the facts on the ground can no longer be reversed. Slow attribution meant no response.
stories.quote: If you're only going to understand a few weeks later. That time it's too late because the Russian army was in full control of Crimea.

stories.topic: Publishing Putin's Invasion Plan in Advance
stories.summary: Before Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the Biden team decided to release its intelligence publicly: the invasion plan, the dates, which tanks would move where. When the invasion came, nobody could plausibly claim it was a local uprising. Ajay calls this the triumph of Western intelligence, in contrast to its failures over Crimea and Iraq.
stories.insight: Intelligence is usually hoarded, but spending it publicly can defeat a lie before it is told. Early, credible attribution leaves the propagandist nothing to work with.
stories.quote: In February 2022, before Putin launched the invasion, the Biden team came up with a brilliant idea that they would just reveal their intelligence in public domain.

stories.topic: Tukaram Omble and the One Terrorist Taken Alive
stories.summary: During the 2008 Mumbai attack, constable Tukaram Omble grappled with Ajmal Kasab on Marine Drive as he tried to get away. Omble kept him from escaping so he could be taken alive, and was shot and killed doing it. Because Kasab survived, India could get the full story of his origins and training and show that this was proxy warfare by Pakistan. Had every attacker died, Pakistan would have kept complete plausible deniability.
stories.insight: In deniable warfare, attribution can depend on a single thread. One constable's sacrifice turned an anonymous terror strike into a documented state-backed operation.
stories.quote: And because we caught Kasab and only because we caught Kasab we managed to get the details and we figured out this was proxy warfare again from Pakistan.

stories.summary: Drawing on Probal Dasgupta's book, Amit says a CIA simulation around 1964 predicted that Pakistan, then booming under Ayub Khan, would attack India in 1966 using proxies. Guerrilla teams would stir a popular uprising in Kashmir while China entered through Sikkim. Pakistan brought the plan forward to August 1965 and sent seven guerrilla teams into Kashmir. It named them after invaders such as Ghaznavi and Babur. The locals saw the infiltrators as foreigners, the uprising never happened, and India pushed them back.
stories.insight: Proxy war is an old Indian experience: 1948, 1965, 2008. It is the weaker side's tool, and it fails when the population you hope to stir up does not see the proxies as its own.
stories.quote: all names of invaders, interestingly, which is kind of weird because what they wanted was they wanted these guerrilla teams to rouse up the local populace and rise up against India.

stories.topic: Sagat Singh Refuses to Withdraw at Nathu La
stories.summary: In 1965 the Indian Army expected China to push through the Sikkim passes, Jelep La and Nathu La, deep into Sikkim. It ordered a pullback so the passes could be defended from wider positions. The general at Jelep La complied. Sagat Singh at Nathu La refused. He reasoned that China might simply want to occupy the high ground, which gives a small force dominance over a larger one below. The Chinese, puzzled that only one pass had been vacated, held off. When fighting came in 1967 at Nathu La and Cho La, they were repelled. Amit argues that a Chinese hold on Nathu La could have cut India off from East Pakistan in 1971.
stories.insight: Good strategy starts with asking what the adversary actually wants. Sagat Singh's disobedience rested on a better reading of Chinese intentions than his orders did, and its payoff came years later.
stories.quote: his thinking was that hey, you are assuming that they will try to come through. What if they just want to occupy?

stories.topic: Shuddh Hindi Propaganda Blasted at Jat Soldiers
stories.summary: At Nathu La in 1967, the Chinese army translated its propaganda into Shuddh Hindi and played it over loudspeakers at Indian troops. Shuddh Hindi is an artificial register that grew out of the 19th-century political split of Hindustani. Nobody speaks it, and the soldiers were Jats who had no idea what was being said. Assuming the broadcasts were working, the Chinese went from four loudspeakers to twelve. The Indians set up their own loudspeakers and somehow shouted counter-propaganda back in Chinese. Amit calls it 'almost like a comic book thing.'
stories.insight: Even in 1967 armies knew information shapes morale. But information warfare is only as good as its model of the audience. Get the language wrong and you can scale up a useless operation with total confidence.
stories.quote: Now, as you and I and every Indian knows, no one in India speaks Shuddh Hindi.

stories.topic: A Real Colorado Rally Organised from St Petersburg
stories.summary: Ajay says there is blow-by-blow evidence that the Internet Research Agency, Yevgeny Prigozhin's outfit in St Petersburg, built up grievance and anger among Americans with targeted messaging. It escalated this all the way to organising a physical Republican protest on the streets of Colorado. He adds that the FBI charged Prigozhin and the IRA over 2016 election interference. Amit accepts that the attempt happened but argues its impact on the election was vastly overstated.
stories.insight: Online influence operations can produce real crowds in real streets, and the aim is less to win an argument than to set citizens against each other. How much such operations actually change outcomes is still debatable.
stories.quote: They fomented the anger, they created the grievance, they baited people with targeted messaging so that people got more and more angry all the way to organizing a physical rally in Colorado.

stories.topic: Russia's Campaign Against India's AstraZeneca Vaccine
stories.summary: The AstraZeneca vaccine was developed by AstraZeneca and Oxford, manufactured at scale by the Serum Institute in India with Gates Foundation help, and protected much of the subcontinent from COVID. Meta documented that in 2021 Russian intelligence ran an influence operation in India to cast doubt on it. The goal was to stop Western institutions from earning Indian goodwill. Amit replies that he had three shots of it and is glad he did.
stories.insight: Information warfare often shows up as an apparently non-political health scare. Some of the strange things trending on the Indian internet are run by foreign powers chasing geopolitical goals.
stories.quote: Because they did not want Indian goodwill in favor of Oxford University and AstraZeneca, a Western Corporation, and the Gates Foundation.

stories.topic: Why Everyone Believed Saddam Had WMD
stories.summary: Amit noted that every intelligence agency, including France's, which opposed the invasion, believed Iraq had weapons of mass destruction. Ajay explains what went wrong. Under a tyrant who would destroy anyone reporting failure, Iraqi civil servants wrote fictional progress reports. Those documents leaked to Western agencies, which trusted the paper. Saddam refused inspections, and only an invading army found that the labs were empty.
stories.insight: In authoritarian systems the regime lies to itself first, so reading its internal documents means reading its lies. Good intelligence needs a sociological understanding of how a state actually works. Ajay compares it to Swachh Bharat toilet counts, where fake numbers flow up a bureaucracy until the top believes them.
stories.quote: So the civil servants wrote on file that, Sir, we have made great progress. We have biological weapons which are killing mice. Next step we will start killing monkeys.

stories.topic: The Hamas Short Position That Wasn't
stories.summary: Ajay billed this as 'the world's best story' for researchers. Soon after the October 7 attack, an American research paper claimed someone had taken a vast short position on Israeli markets just before it. The implication was that the plotters made about half a billion dollars from their own atrocity. Amit said the evil of the attack dwarfs any trading profit anyway. The punchline: the paper had programming errors and the result was wrong.
stories.insight: Terror and private profit can in principle mix, which makes attribution harder still. But a sensational finding deserves suspicion until its code has been checked, a lesson Ajay aims squarely at researchers.
stories.quote: It turned out that there were mistakes in the programming, so the result was actually wrong.

recommendations.item: Watershed 1967: India's Forgotten Victory Over China
recommendations.creator: Probal Dasgupta
recommendations.context: Amit's mid-episode recommendation. He had just recorded an episode with Dasgupta, a popular historian and former Indian Army officer, which was due out a few weeks later.
recommendations.reason: It tells the little-known story of India pushing China back in 1967. Its background chapters supplied several of Amit's stories here: the CIA war game, Pakistan's 1965 guerrilla teams, Sagat Singh at Nathu La, and the Chinese loudspeaker propaganda. It also touches on Chinese backing for the Naxalites.

recommendations.item: Concerns About Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI): An Indian Perspective
recommendations.creator: University of Navarra and XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: Ajay mentions it as his organisation's working paper on foreign interference in elections.
recommendations.reason: It collects global evidence and fragments of hard information about foreign actors around Indian elections. Ajay's point is that India cannot assume hybrid warfare only happens elsewhere.

recommendations.item: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
recommendations.creator: Akshaya Mukul
recommendations.context: Listed in the show notes after Amit cited his conversation with Mukul to push back on blaming India's Hindu-Muslim tensions on foreign interference.
recommendations.reason: It shows that the communal strain has run through Indian society all along. Secular liberals were the fringe, and politics simply caught up with society.

recommendations.item: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (Episode 139 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Akshaya Mukul
recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'a great episode' while arguing that India's fault lines are homegrown.
recommendations.reason: It is the long-form version of his argument that foreign powers can only add to divisions that already exist.

recommendations.creator: Puja Mehra
recommendations.context: Amit cites it while discussing how 26/11 led to Chidambaram's move to the Home Ministry and Pranab Mukherjee's return to Finance.
recommendations.reason: It details how post-2008 economic policy, including retrospective taxation, set the economy sliding from 2011. Amit uses it to argue that no foreign plotter could have foreseen or planned that chain of events.

recommendations.item: The Reformers (Episode 28 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes after Amit said of the Lost Decade story, 'which we have also spoken about.'
recommendations.reason: Background on the policy story behind India's post-2008 slowdown.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit opens by pointing to their earlier Ukraine episodes. Ajay recalls that he left the Wagner Group out of that five-and-a-half-hour recording, then Prigozhin's mutiny forced a follow-up segment.
recommendations.reason: Deep context on the war that drives many of this episode's examples, including drones, 'Uber for artillery', Wagner and Crimea.

recommendations.item: The State of the Ukraine War (Episode 14 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: One of the earlier Ukraine episodes Amit refers to in the intro.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's earlier analysis of the war, on which this hybrid-warfare discussion builds.

core_ideas.concept: The Grey Zone: Detection, Attribution, Response
core_ideas.explanation: War is no longer simply on or off. Between explicit war (Russia and Ukraine) and explicit peace (Japan and the US) lies a grey zone of hostile acts. Hybrid warfare is the craft of harming a rival while staying below the threshold of detection (the victim doesn't know it was attacked) or attribution (it can't tell who did it). Either way, a response becomes hard. There is also a time dimension: detection and attribution usually arrive eventually, so short-term players get their punch in, and the bill comes later.
core_ideas.quote: So the organizing principles are what I've already said, which is show me a hostile action that you could conduct that stays below the detection threshold. Show me a hostile action that can stay below the attribution threshold. Okay, that's the game.

core_ideas.concept: Hybrid Warfare Is the Strategy of the Weak
core_ideas.explanation: A country that cannot fight frontally turns to sneaky, deniable tactics. Russia, with an economy Ajay puts at the size of Italy's, gets outsized returns from cheap hybrid operations. Each small attack, like the Paris cable cuts, carries a veiled threat of bigger ones. That fear strengthens the 'let's just make peace' faction in the target country, as seen in Germany's long softness on Putin.
core_ideas.quote: Hiding inside every small attack is a veiled threat about bigger attacks in the future.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay lists four main tools. (1) Cyber attacks, for example on power grids, routed through friendly countries' IP addresses. (2) Proxies: Wagner, Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed for the ISI, Hamas and Hezbollah for Iran, Russian soldiers posing as Donetsk rebels, and private cyber gangs deliberately grown by Russia and China so governments can blame 'criminals'. (3) Information warfare, where propaganda is old but social media's rabbit holes are the new turning point. (4) Economic coercion and violent acts that stay below the threshold, such as the Baltic anchor drag.
core_ideas.quote: So people have applied themselves to saying what things can I do to harm my enemies without getting to detection or attribution.

core_ideas.explanation: This is a cyber-security term for attackers who are both highly skilled and sustained over time. Teenage 'script kiddies' lack the skill, and private criminals lose interest after one crime. Only states can buy the brainpower and keep at it, so an attack that is both advanced and persistent points to a state, even one hiding behind contracted private gangs.
core_ideas.quote: Private people don't persistently do these things. They'll sort of launch one crime and then they'll lose interest.

core_ideas.explanation: Authoritarian states can keep secrets and act without legislatures, freedom-of-information laws or lawyers, so dirty tricks come easily to them. The CIA, by contrast, is tied down by law at every step. Meanwhile the openness of democracies, now distorted by social media, gives attackers an easy surface to exploit. Attack capability sits with autocracies and the exposure sits with democracies.
core_ideas.quote: So it is much more feasible to launch dirty tricks when you are an authoritarian country. It's much harder for democracies to do covert operations.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit pushed back that India's Hindu-Muslim tensions are homegrown, citing the Gita Press history. Ajay agreed completely: the raw material cannot be invented. Information warfare looks for a society's weak spots and inflames them, such as the Tea Party and Trumpists in America or communal fault lines in India. Hybrid warfare in general works by finding the point of greatest pain, whether that is the Taj and Oberoi in Mumbai or the long, open Baltic seabed.
core_ideas.quote: The problems are homegrown. But it is the nature of information warfare that you will identify the difficulties of the country and pour oxygen on the fires.

core_ideas.concept: Division as a Weapon Against Foreign Policy
core_ideas.explanation: Through the Cold War, Democrats and Republicans differed in degree but agreed the communist bloc had to be confronted. Ajay argues that today pro-Russian views are mainstream in America, which he calls one of Putin's greatest achievements. A country at war with itself cannot mount a coherent response abroad. Amit counters that Putin invaded no one during Trump's first term, and that the Russia-Trump case needs extraordinary evidence.
core_ideas.quote: And at another level, when faced with the difficulties of foreign policy, like you see in the modern United States. if there is a complete internal warfare inside the country, they're not able to mount an effective response.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit warns against reading history backwards, as in '26/11 happened, Chidambaram was moved, the economy tanked, so the ISI planned it.' Foreign interference serves narrow, immediate aims. What follows is a chain of unintended consequences that nobody can foresee. Ajay agrees and cites Karl Popper's argument that complex conspiracy theories are implausible because no small cabal can plan that much. As his example he asks who could have predicted that October 7 would lead to the fall of the Assad regime.
core_ideas.quote: So often taking a teleological view is a problem and often hybrid warfare has all kinds of unintended consequences which go all over the place.

core_ideas.concept: Tactical Wins, Strategic Losses: The Rogue-Nation Bill
core_ideas.explanation: Hawks in the ISI might score 26/11 as a success. But it destroyed global trust in Pakistan: Fortune 500 boards backed away, foreign governments made hundreds of small decisions against it, and its economy suffered from isolation. Hybrid warfare suits leaders who manage headlines rather than countries. At the 'high table' of well-run nations (Norway would never do this to France), such behaviour is off-limits. That is where Ajay says India should aspire to be, which is why he does not see hybrid warfare as optimal for India.
core_ideas.quote: If you play for headlines, if your decision horizon is one week, if you are managing the headlines and not the country.

core_ideas.concept: Intelligence Is the First Line of Defence
core_ideas.explanation: Early detection and attribution weaken an information campaign, because once people know a foreign power is behind it, they discount it. Intelligence has to be sociologically deep, as the Iraq WMD failure shows, and timely, as Crimea shows. The Ukraine 2022 disclosures show what it can achieve. Its scope must also widen beyond traditional war to cover cyber, proxies and influence operations, while accepting that mistakes will still happen.
core_ideas.quote: But if a campaign is detected early and the attribution is done early, then actually the people are reasonably bright.

core_ideas.explanation: The danger lies in reading about the Baltic or Australian elections and assuming nothing is happening in India. Ajay says that by one estimate about 43% of Russia's Ukraine-war influence campaign targeted India. He also cites Russia's anti-AstraZeneca operation, the 2022 attacks on India's power system believed to have come from China, and the AIIMS hack, believed to be Chinese, which exposed the medical records of powerful Indians. His advice is to wake up, without branding every dissident a 'foreign hand.'
core_ideas.quote: So we should not read the foreign press and the lack of knowledge about hybrid warfare that is present in India and conclude that India is safe.

core_ideas.concept: India as the Cyber Attackers' Test Range
core_ideas.explanation: India calls itself an IT superpower, yet Ajay says global attack groups now use it as a training ground. There are plenty of misconfigured systems, and Indian companies tend to hush up breaches instead of reporting them to vendors, so holes stay unpatched. Attackers debug new zero-day exploits on Indian targets before using them on the West. The fix is to raise standards across public and private systems, starting with India's 'abysmal' government software.
core_ideas.quote: So what the global attackers are doing is you first roll out your latest and greatest zero day based attacks on Indian targets, confirm this works, debug your software, and one week later take it into Europe and America.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues that foreign state information warfare is a small part of the wider misinformation problem, most of which he guesses is generated at home. Since attribution is often impossible, the sensible policy is to fight misinformation wherever it comes from, whether China, Russia or 'some guy sitting in UP.' Hybrid warfare thrives because it can blend into that existing sea.
core_ideas.quote: And the point is misinformation is misinformation, we should fight it regardless.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit says most pro-Russian opinion in America is sincerely held, not bought, and a democracy is healthier for having it. Dismissing opposing views as foreign-sponsored is like the Indian government calling dissidents 'anti-national.' His example of the opposite danger is the Hunter Biden laptop affair, where, he argues, mainstream media and Twitter suppressed a true story as 'Russian propaganda.' Covert foreign manipulation is a real but separate problem, and the two should not be conflated.
core_ideas.quote: You know, it is deeply totalitarian to say that my view is right, and any other view is uh you know, some foreign agents are doing it.

core_ideas.concept: Epistemic Institutions Are the Real Defence
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay matches responses to threats: kinetic capability against proxies and terror ('get guns there faster'), better-engineered systems against cyber attacks. For information warfare, the only real defence is a society's ability to establish what is true. That means good data and statistics, universities, researchers, trusted media and believable government bodies. Fact-checkers are only a thin layer on top. Where these institutions are weak, as Ajay says they are in India, every manipulator has a field day. The US came through Cold War propaganda because trusted people spoke up and were believed.
core_ideas.quote: The only way to fight information war is to grow the depth and capability and activism of that epistemic institutional capability.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening: 'we are both men of peace. Shanti Shanti Shanti' who want everyone to love everyone else, 'not in an amorous way, don't get naughty thoughts, but in a platonic way.'

On the Finnish Navy boarding the Chinese tanker, Amit imagines the captain asking 'Who are you and what do you want?' and getting the reply 'We are Finnish, you are finished.' Ajay helpfully notes that his own version of the punchline was 'and you are finished.' Amit protests: 'Always elaborating on jokes... This man, I gotta tell you, freaking analyze the jokes... Can you improve the copywriting?'
Ajay on the Nathu La loudspeaker battle: 'And pre-Google Translate. Spare a thought for the plight of the Indian soldiers trying to create propaganda shouting in Chinese.'

When Ajay announces 'the world's best story,' Amit says he is 'so excited now' because this sounds like his own habit: 'I'm going to tell the world's best story, South Asia's best anecdote.' Ajay replies: 'We are a linear combination of our influences. So you are reshaping my standards of telling stories.'

After the AstraZeneca story, Amit tells Ajay that without the vaccine 'You could have been talking to an empty chair. With sadness in your eyes.' Ajay: 'There would have been no Everything is Everything... Everything is nothing.'

Amit's sign-off: the episode was 'a primer, a wake up call, and a confession,' because Ajay has been waging hybrid warfare on him with fruit, biryani and sweets. 'You're killing me softly with your sugar.' Now wise to the tactic, Amit vows to resist, though Ajay 'may give me coffee and cheese.'
'Uber for artillery': Amit's name for the bottom-up way Ukrainian forces organise artillery and ammunition, alongside drones striking trenches far behind the front lines.

The Sudetenland playbook: Ajay describes the 20th-century template of stirring up a 'rebellion,' recognising the rebels, then answering their plea for help, as when the German army entered Czechoslovakia to 'help oppressed Germans.' Putin used it in Crimea and Donetsk.

Comintern and Voice of America: Ajay's reminder that propaganda is old on both sides of the Cold War. What is new is social media, which gives a power like Russia an ability to work inside democracies that the Comintern never had.
Marine Le Pen's personal loans from Putin, cited by Ajay as an explicit money trail in Russia's funding of nationalist populists in France and Germany.
The Hunter Biden laptop affair, Amit's example of US media and the pre-Musk Twitter suppressing a true story as 'Russian propaganda,' and why a marketplace of ideas matters.
Ajay invokes the 'end of history' mood, a period when the West thought 'everything is going to be hunky-dory' and ignored China's misbehaviour.

'It is Swachh Bharat all over again': Ajay on bureaucracies where fake numbers flow upward until leaders believe them, as in Saddam's Iraq. 'Because a document says we built so many toilets, it doesn't mean you should start cheering.'
Karl Popper's case against complex conspiracy theories, invoked by Ajay: nobody can plan that much, 'least of all a secret small cabal of conspirators.'
Sarajevo: Ajay says no ISI officer can claim, like the man who 'committed one murder in Sarajevo and then the whole world went aflame,' credit for every domino that fell after 26/11.
Ajay asks 'Who could have predicted that the October 7 attack would lead to the fall of the Assad regime?' as an illustration of the law of unintended consequences.
Amit counters the claim that China is being punished for hybrid actions by noting that Saudi Arabia murdered a Washington Post columnist in a foreign country and faced nowhere near that pushback.

Amit's aside on the origin of Shuddh Hindi: a 19th-century political movement split Hindustani, tagged Urdu as Muslim, and stripped Persian-derived words from 'Hindi,' producing a language nobody actually speaks.
